Cherub.name: Cherub
Cherub.publicNotes:
Subjects of stone fountain sculptures and religious paintings throughout the Universe, cherubs are minor celestials who seek to promote cooperation, peace, and above all else, love between mortal creatures. To many cherubs, the goal of nurturing love and affection between two diametrically opposed enemies is the height of bliss. While they have magical abilities and innate spells that can help them in these pursuits, most cherubs consider such methods as tactics of last resort, or tools to be reached for when passion turns to wrath and violence breaks out. Despite their belief in love conquering all, cherubs aren't naive and understand that in some cases, love simply can't bloom. Faced with such a quandary, the cherub instead seeks to minimize conflict, hoping to lay foundations that at some point in the future can lead to a peaceful or, even better, romantic resolution.

While cherubs are kindly, compassionate, and at worst maybe a little mischievous, certain fiends find them to be particularly annoying. These unholy agents of corruption take great pleasure in capturing cherubs and forcing them to act in ways against their very nature, in using magic to disguise themselves as cherubs in order to work their evil deeds while eroding a society's trust in cherubic goodness, or simply relying on particularly realistic illusions to do the same. Using @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.f8SBoXiXQjlCKqly]{Illusory Creature} to create a sinister cherub is a tactic many fiends are quite fond of.

action->Cherub’s Arrow.name: Cherub’s Arrow
action->Cherub’s Arrow.description:
The cherub concentrates on an arrow they have nocked in their bow, imbuing it with supernatural power before firing it at a target within 30 feet. The arrow inflicts no damage on a hit, and instead has one of the following effects, chosen by the cherub. While the cherub can use this ability every round if they so choose, they can never pick the same effect twice in a row. A creature struck must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:16] save or be affected as follows, depending on the cherub's choice (on a critical hit, the creature takes a –2 penalty to the saving throw).

Delight The target becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} as they become distracted by all the wonders of life until the start of the cherub's next turn.

Love The target becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AdPVz7rbaVSRxHFg]{Fascinated} for 1 minute by a second, non-cherub creature within 30 feet of the cherub whom the target can see. This effect has the visual trait.

Peace The target is filled with a sense of tranquility and takes a –1 status penalty to attack rolls for 1 minute.

Regret The target becomes filled with shame and remorse, becoming @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.fesd1n5eVhpCSS18]{Sickened 1} (@UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.fesd1n5eVhpCSS18]{Sickened 2} on a critical failure).

Deravon.name: Deravon
Deravon.publicNotes: The devoted Knights of the Aeon Star who chose to serve in the Sanctum of Aroden believed their tours of duty would last, at most, a few years, and that they would emerge from the sanctum with glory and prestige. In truth, when Aroden died, these knights slowly starved to death after becoming trapped within the Sanctum, only to rise from death when the malevolent forces from the Heart of Sarnax got into their bodies and drew back their souls to serve as sanctum knights. These rare undead are found only in the Sanctum of Aroden.

action->Proof of Undeath.name: Proof of Undeath
action->Proof of Undeath.description: A sanctum knight believes themself to be a living immortal, but if offered proof that they are in fact undead, they must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:20] save or become @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 1} (or @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 3} on a critical failure). On a critical success, they're temporarily immune to this fear for 24 hours. Once they recover from being frightened, their memories of the proof offered fade and they once again regard themselves as living immortals. Proof of undeath includes whenever they take vitality damage, whenever they restore HP as a result of void damage, or whenever a character within 30 feet presents evidence or an argument as a 2-action activity with the linguistic trait and succeeds at a @Check[deception|dc:17], @Check[diplomacy|dc:17], or @Check[intimidation|dc:17] check.

On a failure, his helm topples from his head. While he can move through solid objects while his helm is off, he can't use Aeon Stars or Bow Before Me, and is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.xYTAsEpcJE1Ccni3]{Slowed 1} as long as he remains without his helm.

Fate of the Iomedaeans.name: Fate of the Iomedaeans
Fate of the Iomedaeans.description: From within his sword prison, Meloth unleashes a malign vision that accurately depict the fate of the Iomedaeans who explored this chamber six decades ago. As the PCs experience the vision, the ship shakes and lurches about.
Fate of the Iomedaeans.disable: @Check[religion|dc:17] three times to oppose Meloth's influence and to purge the vision with prayer or @Check[intimidation|dc:20] to establish spiritual dominance over the vision; once disabled in either way, the vision plays out to the end but has no detrimental effects on the PCs from that point forward (although the imps still manifest at the start of round 4 to attack the PCs).
Fate of the Iomedaeans.routine:
(1 action) Each round, the Fate of the Iomedaeans trap takes a different action, as detailed below.

Round 1 Illumination returns to the ship chamber. The ship now rolls on a sea of hellfire, while burning clouds and red lightning fill the sky. Four ghostly humans—Iomedaeans all—appear on the main deck, two against the port rail and two near the prow, manipulating the crystal lens. Their leader stands next to the wheel in area B20, while the House of Secrets wizard who accompanies them is up in the crow's nest. He has the irezoko tattooed on his face, a different design than the one on Sarnax's statues, but definitely in the same tradition. Each PC must succeed at a @Check[reflex|dc:17] save or be knocked @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.j91X7x0XSomq8d60]{Prone} by the rolling motion of the ship.

Round 2 The ship rolls more violently on the sea of fire. Each PC must succeed at a @Check[reflex|dc:17] save or be knocked @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.j91X7x0XSomq8d60]{Prone}. Those who critically fail are thrown overboard and appear to burn to ashes in the sea of fire (in actuality, they are merely tossed overboard and fall 15 feet to the floor below in area B12, taking normal falling damage). A PC can attempt a @Check[reflex|dc:15] save to [[/act grab-an-edge]] to prevent this fall by clinging to a ship's railing.

Round 3 The phantom image of a vordine devil appears in a cloud of brimstone at the center of the deck, just aft of the main mast. The PCs can smell the brimstone, but the devil itself appears ephemeral, like the Iomedaeans. The armored clerics begin drawing weapons and casting spells. The PCs cannot directly interact with these figures, but the manifestation of the devil is unsettling—all PCs in the area must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:17] save to avoid becoming @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 1} (@UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 2} on a critical failure); this is an emotion, fear, and mental effect.

Round 4 At the start of this round, Meloth unleashes a gang of imps from the dimensional prison within Meloth's Lifedrinker, controlling them to roll up over both sides of the ship and onto the main deck. The imps roll initiative and join the encounter, attacking the PCs and ignoring the illusions. The two clerics manipulating the prow lens yell at the wizard in the crow's nest. "The lens is powering the ship's phase spike! How can we travel without the helm? How do we make it stop?" they plead. The ship rolls again, this time in the opposite direction. One of the Iomedaeans at the rail spills over the side, vanishing in hellfire. The vordine takes advantage of her companion's distraction and runs another Iomedaean through, killing her with a single blow of its jagged glaive. Two of the imps cast invisibility and then fly over to land next to a different PC in hopes of stinging them the next round. The other two imps each attempt to cast charm on a different PC, then Fly into positions above those PCs. At the end of the round, each PC must succeed at a @Check[reflex|dc:17] save or be knocked @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.j91X7x0XSomq8d60]{Prone} (but without the danger of being thrown overboard this time). The two imps who cast invisibility must also attempt this save to avoid being knocked prone; the flying imps take @Damage[(1d6+3)[bludgeoning]] damage from being battered by the mast, rigging, railing, or other portions of the ship (@Check[reflex|dc:17|basic] save).

Round 5 The ship rights itself again, and the vordine closes with the two clerics at the bow. From the crow's nest, the wizard blasts a bolt of lightning at the devil. The vordine deflects the spell with a casual wave of its claw (a dramatic flourish added by Meloth), and an electric shock surges through the planks of the main deck to arc through the rigging. Each PC and each imp takes @Damage[(1d6+3)[electricity]] damage (@Check[reflex|dc:17|basic] save). During this round, all the imps land and attack different PCs.

Round 6 The vordine kills both of the Iomedaeans near the crystal lens. From the crow's nest, the wizard screams at the Iomedaean leader, who still attends the wheel. Black smoke pours from her mouth and eyes. PCs who succeed at a @Check[perception|dc:20] check notice a shadowy, winged, one-eyed form looming over her, whispering into her ear (a shadowy manifestation of Meloth himself). She deliberately turns the wheel sharply, pitching the Provarion forward desperately, resulting in another violent shift akin to the one that occurs on round 2 (potentially throwing PCs and imps overboard).

Round 7 The vordine translocates from the ship's bow up into the crow's nest. The wizard's screams are cut off as the devil lops off his head, which topples down to the main deck, taking two awkward bounces before landing at the feet of a PC (if possible, a PC with the Mystery Adept background). That PC sees the wizard's lips move and believes the head is mouthing a threat of "I see ye!" The PC must attempt a @Check[will|dc:17] save to avoid becoming @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 1} (@UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 2} and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.sDPxOjQ9kx2RZE8D]{Fleeing} as long as they remain frightened on a critical failure); a PC who has the Read Lips feat realizes that instead the wizard was mouthing a hopeless cry of "Save me!" and automatically gets a success on the Will save.

Round 8 The vordine translocates down to the ship's wheel. The phantom figure behind the Iomedaean leader vanishes like smoke (assuming the PCs ever saw it in the first place) as the devil appears in its place. As the vordine runs the leader through from behind, killing her with his trident, the devil seems to look directly into the eyes of each observer. Each PC must attempt a @Check[will|dc:17] save to avoid becoming @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.3uh1r86TzbQvosxv]{Doomed 1}; this has the emotion, fear, mental, and visual traits.

Round 9 The haunt ends, but the imps continue to fight to the death if any still live.

action->We're all in Hell!.description:
Trigger Three living creatures are in area B18 at the same time

The haunt then rolls initiative.

Heart of Sarnax.name: Heart of Sarnax
Heart of Sarnax.publicNotes: When Sarnax sought to purge his soul of all evils, the result was a physical manifestation of crystal that approximated the size and shape of his heart. The evil contained within remained quiescent as long as Sarnax lived, but upon his death, the item gained power, no longer held in check by Sarnax's living soul. If returned to any version of the living Sarnax, this grown evil manifests into a creature made of solid ruby whose first and primary goal is the destruction of its source. Afterward, the Heart of Sarnax can turn its attention to the world, eager to visit upon reality all the evils, both petty and potent, that Sarnax might have pursued had he fallen from grace while alive.

action->Hear Heartbeat.name: Hear Heartbeat
action->Hear Heartbeat.description: The Heart of Sarnax can hear a living creature's heartbeat as a precise sense in the listed range.

action->Speak to Inner Evils.name: Speak to Inner Evils
action->Speak to Inner Evils.description:
Frequency once per round

Effect The Heart of Sarnax speaks to a creature it can hear the heartbeat of within 60 feet, beckoning that creature to give in to their inner desires to commit evil acts. The Heart of Sarnax attempts an Intimidation check against the target's Will DC, with the following results.

Critical Success The inner evils take over fully, and the target becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.yblD8fOR1J8rDwEQ]{Confused} for 1 minute. While confused, the creature will never attack the Heart of Sarnax, attacking themself instead if the Heart of Sarnax is the only viable target. The Heart of Sarnax becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.nlCjDvLMf2EkV2dl]{Quickened} for 1 round, and can use the extra action only to Speak to Inner Evils.

Success The inner evils take over only briefly. The creature becomes confused for 1 round.

Failure The inner evils fail to take over fully but are still distracting. The creature becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} until the end of their next turn.

Critical Failure The creature resists their inner evils and is immune to Speak to Inner Evils from this point on. The Heart of Sarnax recoils in shock, taking @Damage[4d6[mental]] damage (@Check[will|dc:25|basic] save).

action->Void Beam.name: Void Beam
action->Void Beam.description: The Heart of Sarnax fires a @Template[type:line|distance:60] of spiraling, shadowy void energy from the cavity in its chest. Creatures in the area take @Damage[7d6[void]|options:area-damage] damage (@Check[fortitude|dc:24|basic]). For many societies, ogres embody brutish, amoral violence and greedy cruelty. Standing 10 feet tall and densely muscled, ogres are usually as strong as they are vicious. The worst ogres are sadists, enjoying remorseless murder, torture, and violence in all of its forms. Although they prefer to vent their violent urges on other humanoids—the smaller the better—ogre captivity can end in a horrifying fate for anyone unlucky enough to fall within their meaty grasp: becoming dinner. But for all their creativity in inflicting pain, ogres often forget that their playthings lack their own robust fortitude and high pain tolerance, and many of their captives die sooner than the ogres might prefer. Meanwhile, those who manage to survive captivity in an ogre's larder often emerge with lasting mental scars. A captive able to keep their wits about them, however, can sometimes trick the brutes by promising treasure, more plentiful food sources, or other crude amusements, taking advantage of an ogre's often-limited intellect to engineer opportunities to escape or gain revenge.

Ogres are social creatures only in the most debased sense. They gather together in groups called families, though members are not always related by blood. The most powerful ogre in any family is the "boss"—usually the family's patriarch or matriarch—whom the other ogres in the family learn to quickly obey or risk being brutalized by the boss's loyal kin. Ogres lair in caves, crumbling ruins, or dilapidated shacks close enough to humanoid settlements or animal trails to make raiding easy. Their lairs are filthy and frequently contain all-too-recognizable evidence of their depravity, along with assorted treasures stolen from past captives.

Provarion.name: Provarion
Provarion.description:
The Provarion is an astounding work of magical engineering known as an ether ship. These vessels were highly valued in ancient Azlant for their capability of traveling between planes. The most famous ether ship was an immense vessel called King Xeros of Old Azlant, but other smaller ether ships like the Provarion existed as well. The exact capabilities of each ether ship varied, but they were similar in many ways to those of the Provarion.

The Provarion functions fully well as a sailing ship even without any of its magical abilities. The fact that, as an ether ship, the Provarion is highly resistant to destruction certainly gave it an advantage to those who would ply dangerous waters, but such protection wouldn't have protected the ship from being swamped, capsized, or dragged to the bottom of the sea by rogue waves, powerful storms, or immense sea monsters. Other ether ships met such fates, but the Provarion's destiny was to be buried below Absalom in the Sanctum of Aroden.

As with all ether ships, the Provarion's magical abilities cannot be activated unless three smaller artifacts—a cubic helm, a set of ether sails, and a phase spike—are installed in the ship. (The supernaturally light ether sails are still 10 Bulk, the 15-foot-long phase spike is 8 Bulk, and the missing cubic helm is 2 Bulk.) In the Provarion's case, two of these artifacts can be found on deck, but the third, a cubic helm, is missing. These three items are interchangeable between ether ships, so one could, in theory, salvage replacements from other ether ships—if such ships could even be found in the first place. These three artifacts have no function on their own and must be installed in an ether ship like the Provarion to grant it's activations.

Destruction The Provarion can be destroyed if it is used to sail into the heart of the Maelstrom and is then used to travel to Creation's Forge—doing so reduces the ship to raw soulstuff and scatters any incidental items and creatures on board across the Great Beyond, with the exception of the ship's cubic helm, ether sails, and phase spike: these artifacts are destroyed as well alongside the Provarion.

If the ship isn't flying at the time, it appears on the closest body of liquid capable of supporting it within 1d20 × 25 miles of your destination—or if no such body of liquid is available, it becomes beached on the ground. Reglok.publicNotes:
Among the subtler of the alghollthu creations were the ugothols—also known as faceless stalkers. These twisted beings used shapeshifting to infiltrate settlements and assassinate key targets. They sowed discord and replaced leaders, causing unwanted organizations to implode and bothersome people to lose face and eventually disappear.

In bygone millennia, aquatic monsters known as alghollthus used their occult powers to conquer and rule vast swaths of the world. Alghollthus shaped their servitors and other creatures using mental manipulation and physically transformative magic. The rulers of the alghollthus, the so-called "veiled masters," further shaped entire societies by assuming the forms of those they controlled.

In time, the alghollthus grew frustrated with upstart surface societies and meddling gods. They used incredible magical power to call forth a cataclysm, hoping to destroy the rebellious societies they'd manipulated. Yet they miscalculated the will to survive of those they treated as their pawns, and in time the world recovered, this time free of alghollthu influence.

Today, the alghollthus have mostly remained within the deep aquatic realms where they still rule without question. Yet they have not abandoned their plots entirely, and the reemergence of servitors like faceless stalkers suggests that the alghollthus have turned their hateful eyes to the surface once again.

Sanctum Knight.name: Sanctum Knight
Sanctum Knight.publicNotes: The devoted Knights of the Aeon Star who chose to serve in the Sanctum of Aroden believed their tours of duty would last, at most, a few years, and that they would emerge from the sanctum with glory and prestige. In truth, when Aroden died, these knights slowly starved to death after becoming trapped within the Sanctum, only to rise from death when the malevolent forces from the Heart of Sarnax got into their bodies and drew back their souls to serve as sanctum knights. These rare undead are found only in the Sanctum of Aroden.

action->Proof of Undeath.name: Proof of Undeath
action->Proof of Undeath.description: A sanctum knight believes themself to be a living immortal, but if offered proof that they are in fact undead, they must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:20] save or become @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 1} (or @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TBSHQspnbcqxsmjL]{Frightened 3} on a critical failure). On a critical success, they're temporarily immune to this fear for 24 hours. Once they recover from being frightened, their memories of the proof offered fade and they once again regard themselves as living immortals. Proof of undeath includes whenever they take vitality damage, whenever they restore HP as a result of void damage, or whenever a character within 30 feet presents evidence or an argument as a 2-action activity with the linguistic trait and succeeds at a @Check[deception|dc:17], @Check[diplomacy|dc:17], or @Check[intimidation|dc:17] check.

The Doom of Azlant.name: The Doom of Azlant
The Doom of Azlant.description: Fiery rocks from space crash through the skylight ceiling of the Azlanti throne room, showering those below in ceaseless cascades of fire and broken glass.
The Doom of Azlant.disable: This is the end of days. The Doom of Azlant cannot be disabled or averted in any way.
The Doom of Azlant.routine:
(1 action) At the end of each round, starting on round 7, roll 1d8 to determine which section of the throne room of Azlant is struck by another Falling Star, rerolling results that indicate sections that have already been destroyed. The Falling Star destroys that section of the room, as well as any undestroyed pillars potentially containing veiled masters. Non-statted NPCs in that room section are killed instantly, consumed by otherworldly flame and crushed by flying debris. All PCs, palace guards, and vidileths not currently in a pillar who are in the room segment take @Damage[(2d6+4)[bludgeoning]] damage and @Damage[2d6[fire]] damage (@Check[reflex|dc:24|basic] save). A critical failure also knocks the creature @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.j91X7x0XSomq8d60]{Prone}.

Destroyed room sections function as difficult terrain, but also pose additional dangers. The first time during a character's turn that they take any action with the move trait that takes place wholly or partially in a destroyed room segment, roll [[/r 1d6]] and consult the following additional dangers to see what that character must endure as a result of their movement.

1–2 Desperate Courtier Seemingly from out of nowhere, one of the servants or lesser nobles @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.sDPxOjQ9kx2RZE8D]{Fleeing} in terror leaps upon the character, desperately clinging to their clothing and limbs and making movement more difficult. The character can avoid the courtier with a successful @Check[reflex|dc:24] save, otherwise the character takes a –10-foot circumstance penalty to their Speed until they can [[/act escape dc=20]] from the desperate courtier's clutches. Vidileths ignore this result, as no courtier is desperate enough to cling to one of these monsters!

3–4 Hail of Meteorites A bright red barrage of scalding space debris pummels the character for @Damage[(1d6+4)[bludgeoning]] damage and @Damage[1d6[fire]] damage, with additional effects determined by a @Check[reflex|dc:24] save.

Critical Success The creature takes no damage.

Success The creature takes half damage.

Failure The creature takes full damage and is knocked @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.j91X7x0XSomq8d60]{Prone}.

Critical Failure The creature takes full damage, is knocked prone, and takes an additional @Damage[2d6[persistent,fire]] damage.

5–6 Shearing Glass A razor-sharp sheet of jagged green glass tumbles down from the ceiling and threatens to bisect the victim. The creature takes @Damage[2d6[slashing]] damage, with additional effects determined by a @Check[reflex|dc:24] save. If the slashing damage from the glass reduces a creature to 0 HP, a pane of glass shears straight through the victim's neck, slicing off their head and killing them instantly.

Critical Success The creature takes no damage.

Success The creature takes half damage.

Failure The creature takes full damage and @Damage[1d6[persistent,bleed]] damage.

Critical Failure The creature takes double damage and @Damage[2d6[persistent,bleed]] damage.

Ugothol Wretch.name: Ugothol Wretch
Ugothol Wretch.publicNotes:
Among the subtler of the alghollthu creations were the ugothols—also known as faceless stalkers. These twisted beings used shapeshifting to infiltrate settlements and assassinate key targets. They sowed discord and replaced leaders, causing unwanted organizations to implode and bothersome people to lose face and eventually disappear.

In bygone millennia, aquatic monsters known as alghollthus used their occult powers to conquer and rule vast swaths of the world. Alghollthus shaped their servitors and other creatures using mental manipulation and physically transformative magic. The rulers of the alghollthus, the so-called "veiled masters," further shaped entire societies by assuming the forms of those they controlled.

In time, the alghollthus grew frustrated with upstart surface societies and meddling gods. They used incredible magical power to call forth a cataclysm, hoping to destroy the rebellious societies they'd manipulated. Yet they miscalculated the will to survive of those they treated as their pawns, and in time the world recovered, this time free of alghollthu influence.

Today, the alghollthus have mostly remained within the deep aquatic realms where they still rule without question. Yet they have not abandoned their plots entirely, and the reemergence of servitors like faceless stalkers suggests that the alghollthus have turned their hateful eyes to the surface once again.

Vidileth.name: Vidileth
Vidileth.publicNotes:
The powerful vidileths are the insidious veiled masters of the alghollthus. These manipulators of mind and body alike lead their species in the open, using their ability to change form to walk among and deceive humans and other sapient species. Many veiled masters are even more powerful than the typical specimen presented here and can use a wide range of arcane or occult spells and rituals. While veiled masters command significant combat prowess and impressive magical skills, the greatest danger they pose to others is their uncanny ability to infiltrate into societies much different than their own. The most paranoid of adventurers and conspiracy scholars worry that every major city has been infested by secret cabals of vidileths, while others dismiss this as hogwash and fearmongering. The truth is likely somewhere in between, but it doesn't take many veiled masters pulling the strings behind the scenes to wreak havoc upon an entire nation!

In bygone millennia, aquatic monsters known as alghollthus used their occult powers to conquer and rule vast parts of the world. Their empires contained countless mortal slaves treated as little more than cattle. Alghollthus shaped their slaves and other creatures using mental manipulation and physically transformative magic. Aberrant horrors from faceless stalkers to mimics can be traced back to this meddling. The rulers of the alghollthu race, the so-called veiled masters, further shaped entire societies by assuming the forms of those they controlled. From the heights of power to the shadows of poverty, the veiled masters manipulated these societies according to their own dark designs, enslaving, killing, or horrifically transforming those who discovered their plans or acted against them.

In time, the alghollthus grew frustrated with their increasingly upstart slave societies and sought to wipe the slate clean-both starting anew and punishing those who had become too willful and rebellious. They used incredible magical power to call forth a cataclysm, hoping to destroy the rebellious societies they'd manipulated. Yet they miscalculated the strength of faith and will to survive of their pawns and slaves, and in time the world and its empires recovered and grew strong once again-this time without alghollthu influence.

Today, the alghollthus have retreated from their mass-scale manipulation of the surface world, and they have mostly remained within the deep aquatic realms where they still rule without question. Yet they have not abandoned their plots entirely, and the reemergence of servitor races like ugothols points to a frightening possibility-that the alghollthus have turned their hateful eyes to the surface once again.

In the vision, the triggering creature suddenly sees monstrous, shadowy figures flitting about the ship's deck—mechanical men, amorphous blobs, reptilian giants, and so on. The figures move at irregular, inconsistent speeds and intersect one another at times, as if the viewer is watching a series of recorded images taken over decades interposed atop one another and replayed all at once.

In their mind, the sitter hears several whispering voices speaking to them at once in a dozen different languages. Many sound human, but others sound like the turning of cranks, the sibilance of a swarm of snakes, the buzzing of insects, and stranger. Anyone capable of speaking even a single language can make out the gist of what the voices are saying—"take me home," "release us from our prison," and so on. A particularly loud voice calls out: "Seize the cubic helm. Release the ship. Let yourself go, and we will show you how."

Weary.name: Weary
Weary.publicNotes:
While the method of creating the weary is a well-kept secret of hryngar worshippers of Droskar, there's nothing preventing other unholy spellcasters from transforming those who have worked themselves into an early grave into these pitiful, unsettling monsters. The weary don't understand that they've died, only that they're overwhelmed with a deep, aching exhaustion that fills them with a wretched hatred. Content to lie in a slowly rotting heap until they sense the approach of living creatures, when the weary lurch into activity it is with cries of pain and hopelessness. These undead creatures appear as rotting corpses who creep and crawl about on all fours, bodies too worn out to properly hold themselves fully upright.

Unlike zombies, which the weary are sometimes mistaken for, these undead retain their minds and memories of the final several agonizing weeks that led up to their deaths. They can rarely remember farther back than these final weeks and almost never remember their own names. While they're capable of communication, they typically have nothing more to say then to moan and agonize over their pain, and to beg those they attack to end their suffering even as they do their best to chew and gnaw at the living meat that vexes them so.

Zulgara.name: Zulgara
Zulgara.publicNotes:
Deep beneath the surface, the dour dwarves known as hryngars stubbornly toil, claiming the ancestral subterranean homelands of other dwarves as their own. Long ago, hryngar leaders refused to venture to the surface along with their "cousins," forsaking the Quest for Sky. An exiled dwarven deity named Droskar offered hryngars salvation from the horrors that beset them in the Darklands, offering them power, cunning, and knowledge in exchange for their unending servitude. Many hryngar believe that by working harder than their brethren, they can build a society far greater than anything under the sun, claiming unending riches from the planet's metallic veins in days of relentless toil.

Through Droskar's blessings and their own fearsome work ethic, hryngar kingdoms now rule a significant portion of the upper Darklands region of NarVoth, and it's common to see hryngar caravans moving through the tunnels, drawn by teams of immense beetles. Hryngar leadership typically consists of powerful divine servants of Droskar, along with fearsomely implacable warriors whose martial prowess, backed by innate occult magic, ensures they can overcome any direct threat to hryngar rule. Almost every aspect of hryngar society is controlled by a strict hierarchy of leadership, with taskmasters directing subordinates across all walks of life.
